The significant differences in tax rates and funding levels between districts continues to negatively impact  communities like Claremont. And the state's failure to adequately address this problem and adequately fund public education, despite court orders to do so, leads to districts with less property valuation having to tax themselves at higher rates than districts with higher property valuation in order to achieve comparable funding and student outcomes. It's the elephant in the room when it comes to struggling through our budget process, our deliberative session, and ultimately, when voters have to make tough choices between school funding and tax payments. Districts with lower property values continue to struggle, while communities with higher property values generate more funding for their schools. And this flies in the face of the demands of several court cases and results in very difficult decisions when it comes to providing the best education for our children. Now, this is not new. For many of us. This has been an on again, off again thing for  a number of years. So long, in fact, that people have become fatigued, disconnected. And multiple. Court cases of found over the years that New Hampshire education funding is a responsibility that lies with the state, and in its current form, it's inequitable, does not meet constitutional mandates, and presents unfair funding challenges to students, to schools and to taxpayers alike. It affects our budgets, the programs and the staff we'd like to fund. Some of which we've heard about tonight from Mr. Nestor. And it affects outcomes we hope to achieve for our kids. The courts have handed the issue over and over to the legislature for solutions, and despite the findings, the cost of adequacy has not been defined. And for years, the resources that the state provides to local communities like Claremont have fallen far short of what schools actually cost to fund.

role: Ward 3 resident presenting the NH School Funding Fairness Project; SRVRTC Visioning Committee — surname not stated in this record (rendered 'Andy Bernier' 2/8/23 and 'Andy LaFrance' 12/1/23 elsewhere; unreconciled)
text: The difference is down shifted and made up through local property taxes, and that situation creates significant difficulties for towns with lower property values, whose residents desiring comparable outcomes have to rely on disproportionately high local property taxes to fund adequate school budgets that are often already cut to the bone. And those discussions can be quite painful at deliberative sessions that we've all been a part of. So that's dynamic is what the courts have identified as a problem. It's still a problem despite even a very thorough report delivered to the state in 2020 by a commission that was convened to study it and proposed solutions. They did, and those findings have not been meaningfully explored. And so the New Hampshire School Funding Fairness Project, which is a nonprofit, nonpartisan advocacy group, works around New Hampshire to raise awareness of the challenges with New Hampshire school funding and advocates for discussions among the public and among legislators that could lead to a more equitable system. They will be presenting in Claremont on May 25th at 6:30 p.m. at the Claremont Savings Bank Community Center. It'll be a Claremont specific discussion, and attendees will have the opportunity to learn how school funding works, how that impacts students and taxpayers and our communities, and what can be done to facilitate improvement. text: Thank you for this opportunity to speak to you today about youth in government. I'm Aubrey Herzog and I'm a junior at Stevens. And I've been this club for three years. And I think this is by far, like one of the coolest experiment experiences that Stevens has to offer.  The program is through the YMCA, and high school students in New Hampshire take over the state capitol for two days. We sit in the committee rooms, the House and Senate chambers, the New Hampshire Supreme Court,  and even the governor's office. So this year, I ran for the position of youth governor, and this was a unique opportunity to run my own campaign, give speeches, and network with kids my age. I was able to share what I wanted to do to improve the program and go through an interview by the press corps without knowing the questions beforehand. It gives you the opportunity to actively participate in government, even when you're not old enough to vote. I believe the best way to learn about government is through holding a mock one. This year, I was a committee chair for the Health and Human Services Committee. I chaired bills ranging from artificial intelligence, raising the legal marriage age, making seatbelt mandatory for everyone, proper grooming, which was a bill that required everyone in the state to be bald, and legalizing euthanasia.

speaker: Charlene Lovett
role: Mayor, City of Claremont
text: Address to the members of the House Education Committee on behalf of the Claremont City Council and the Claremont School Board. I support HB 525, the annual Reduction of Education Stabilization grants will not only negatively impact the school district's ability to deliver an adequate education, but also the city's economic growth. Though we are independent governing bodies, we are dependent upon the same tax base, which has been stressed in recent years due to a number of factors to include a loss in city valuation, decreased state aid and rising personnel costs. During our last revaluation, Claremont lost approximately $110 million in valuation, increasing our tax rate over $5 due to a decrease in state aid overall. Claremont is now responsible for a greater portion of employee retirement benefits, higher percentages of capital improvement costs, and an increased share  of educational costs. In addition, rising health insurance costs and the need to pay competitive wages has resulted in personnel budgetary increases. These factors have contributed to Claremont holding the highest tax rate in New Hampshire, and the ability of our tax base to fund more increases is exhausted. In recognizing this, the city recently halted any spending of discretionary funds, any hiring freeze. In addition, we are considering a 5% budget decrease for the upcoming year. Currently, the Claremont School Board is making cuts to its budget so that there will be no impact to the tax rate in FY 18.
